title: “DO NOT BE MISLED” — THE WARNING WE KEEP SKIPPING BEFORE “BAD COMPANY”
paragraphs: “DO NOT BE MISLED” — THE WARNING WE KEEP SKIPPING BEFORE “BAD COMPANY”
Paul was warning about something more dangerous than having the wrong friends. He was exposing what happens when a lie gets close enough to reshape what you believe—and eventually, how you live.
There is a frightening way to lose your faith without ever announcing that you have lost it.
You can still know the worship songs.
Still post Bible verses.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still attend church.
Still call yourself a Christian.
And yet, somewhere beneath everything people can see, something has begun to shift.
Not suddenly.
Quietly.
A conviction you once guarded becomes something you negotiate.
A sin that once disturbed you becomes something you explain.
A truth you once defended becomes something you are embarrassed to say out loud.
Prayer becomes occasional.
Repentance becomes uncomfortable.
Holiness begins to sound extreme.
And Jesus remains somewhere in your vocabulary while slowly being moved away from the throne of your life.
Then one day you look at yourself and wonder:
“How did I get this far?”
Paul understood how.
That is why, in the middle of one of the most magnificent chapters ever written about the resurrection of Jesus Christ, he suddenly gives the Corinthian believers a warning:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε· φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί.
Mē planasthe; phtheirousin ēthē chrēsta homiliai kakai.
“Do not be misled: Bad company corrupts good character.”
—1 Corinthians 15:33
But we often begin reading Paul’s warning too late.
We remember “bad company.”
We make it a lesson about choosing good friends.
There is truth in that application.
But look at what Paul was actually discussing.
Resurrection.
Paul was defending the bodily resurrection of the dead because some among the Corinthians were saying there was no resurrection.
And Paul understood something many people still underestimate:
What you believe about eternity will eventually influence how you live today.

If Christ has not been raised, Paul argues, Christian preaching collapses. Faith collapses. The apostles become false witnesses. Those who died in Christ are lost. Christians become pitiable people clinging to an illusion.
But Paul has already thundered the truth earlier in the chapter:
Christ has been raised from the dead.
The resurrection is not decorative theology.
It changes everything.
And immediately before Paul says, “Do not be misled,” he exposes the logical destination of a life emptied of resurrection hope:
“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
That is the atmosphere surrounding the warning.
Then:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε.
Do not be misled.
Do not be deceived.
Do not allow yourself to be led astray.
The Greek verb πλανάω carries the idea of wandering, misleading, or causing someone to stray.
That makes Paul’s opening words deeply uncomfortable.
Because wandering rarely feels like wandering at first.
Nobody wakes up intending to become spiritually cold.
Nobody usually says, “Today I will slowly destroy my convictions.”
It happens through inches.
One conversation.
One compromise.
One voice you keep listening to.
One relationship whose approval matters a little too much.
One philosophy repeated until it stops sounding dangerous.
One sin renamed as freedom.
One biblical conviction dismissed as outdated.
One little surrender after another.
Until the person who once asked, “Lord, what do You want?” begins asking, “How much can I get away with?”
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε.
Paul puts the warning before the explanation because deception is dangerous precisely because the deceived person often does not realize what is happening.
That should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Who has your ear?
What shapes your imagination?
Whose approval are you afraid to lose?
What voices do you repeatedly consume?
What conversations leave you loving Christ more—and which ones slowly make obedience seem ridiculous?
This verse reaches farther than the contacts saved in your phone.
The Greek word translated “company,” ὁμιλίαι (homiliai), can refer to associations, companionships, intercourse, or conversation.
Think about what that means in a world Paul never saw technologically, but whose human heart he understood perfectly.
Some people spend hours every day in the company of people they have never physically met.
The voice in your headphones is company.
The person you watch night after night is influencing you.
The group chat is company.
The feed you scroll when nobody is watching is feeding something.
The voices you continually welcome into your mind do not need a chair at your dinner table to have a seat in your heart.
And Paul does not say bad associations merely inconvenience good character.
He uses:
φθείρουσιν — phtheirousin.
Corrupt.
Spoil.
Ruin.
There is deterioration in the word.
And deterioration can be quiet.
Wood does not announce when rot begins inside it.
Metal does not scream when corrosion starts.
The soul can become accustomed to things that once made it tremble.
That is what makes spiritual drift terrifying.
You may not notice what is disappearing because it disappears gradually.
You stop praying before you admit you stopped depending on God.
You stop confessing before you admit you stopped fighting.
You stop opening Scripture before you admit other voices have become more interesting than His.
You stop grieving over sin before you ever call it acceptable.
And eventually you can become comfortable with something you once begged Jesus to deliver you from.
Maybe that sentence hurts.
Good.
Not because condemnation is the goal.
Because awakening is.
Paul does not stop at verse 33.
His next words are urgent:
“Wake up” to righteousness and stop sinning.
There it is.
Not merely:
Find nicer friends.
Wake up.
This is a resurrection chapter, and Paul is calling spiritually drowsy people back to sober living in light of resurrection truth.
Maybe someone reading this needs that command today.
Wake up.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret night.
Not after the relationship destroys what remains of your convictions.
Not when consequences finally become painful enough.
Wake up.
You know the thing you keep defending.
You know the influence you keep excusing.
You know the conversation that keeps dragging your imagination somewhere Jesus never called you to live.
You know what you delete.
You know what you hide.
You know the version of yourself people at church never see.
And Christ knows too.
But here is where the Gospel changes this article completely.
Jesus did not come merely to expose wanderers.
He came to save them.
Christianity is not the story of morally impressive people protecting themselves from morally inferior people.
Christianity is the story of sinners rescued by a holy Savior.
Every Christian is someone who needed mercy.
Every redeemed life began with grace.
And the resurrection Paul defends in 1 Corinthians 15 is precisely why your story does not have to end where your sin has taken you.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Sin did not defeat Him.
Death did not keep Him.
The grave did not rewrite His identity.
Jesus walked out victorious.
And because the risen Christ saves, repentance is not walking toward hopelessness.
It is coming home.
Maybe you wandered.
Come home.
Maybe you compromised.
Come home.
Maybe you became someone you promised God you would never become again.
Come home.
Maybe pornography returned.
Maybe bitterness hardened.
Maybe pride took over.
Maybe the relationship became your god.
Maybe success became your god.
Maybe people's approval became your god.
Maybe you learned how to appear spiritually alive while privately starving.
Come home.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will reconsider you.”
The Gospel announces a Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved.
Grace brings us to the One who breaks chains.
Repentance is not payment for forgiveness.
Christ paid.
Repentance turns from sin toward the Savior whose mercy we could never purchase.
And maybe this is the scandal someone needs to hear:
Your worst chapter does not have greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted His people.
The Corinthian church itself was painfully messy.
Yet Christ was still building His church out of people transformed by grace.
That does not make sin small.
It makes Jesus magnificent.
This is why the Gospel Warrior message remains:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ can take a human story shattered by sin and write redemption where everyone expected only ruin.
Jesus rewrites everything.
And now Paul's warning becomes intensely personal.
Who are you becoming because of what you continually allow around you?
Not merely:
“Are these people bad?”
Ask something harder.
“Is this drawing me toward Christ or training my heart away from Him?”
Because sometimes the company corrupting you is not a rebellious friend.
Sometimes it is an ideology.
Sometimes it is entertainment.
Sometimes it is your secret digital life.
Sometimes it is bitterness disguised as discernment.
Sometimes it is a Christian circle where everyone talks about other people's sins but nobody confesses their own.
Sometimes it is a relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience, but loneliness makes you terrified to release it.
And sometimes…
you have become bad company for yourself.
You keep rehearsing the same lie.
“I'll never change.”
“God must be finished with me.”
“I've gone too far.”
“I might as well keep sinning.”
No.
Do not be misled.
If you belong to Christ, your future is not ultimately determined by the voice of your shame.
It is anchored in the risen Jesus.
So guard what shapes you.
Choose people who can love you enough to tell you the truth.
Stay near believers who make holiness desirable, Scripture precious, prayer natural, repentance normal, grace astonishing, and Jesus beautiful.
And become that person for someone else.
Not self-righteous.
Not suspicious of every unbeliever.
Jesus Himself ate with sinners and was known for receiving them.
Christians are not called to disappear from the world.
We are called to belong so completely to Christ that while we love people in the world, we do not allow the world's rebellion against God to disciple us.
There is a difference between loving someone and letting them lead you.
There is a difference between reaching people and being reshaped by them.
There is a difference between sitting with sinners to show them Jesus and sitting under sin until you forget why you needed Jesus.
Someone you love may need this warning.
Be honest.
Your honesty may become permission for another wounded believer to stop pretending.
Not because you need another saved post.
Because there may come a night when the compromise looks harmless again.
Come back.
Read Paul's words again:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε.
Do not be misled.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to buy salvation.
Jesus cannot be purchased, and grace cannot be bought.
But Christians are called to generosity, and ministries that continually teach, create, publish, disciple, and reach people require real support to continue their work.
Send it privately to someone drifting.
Comment so another person realizes they are not fighting alone.
Because somebody's eternity is worth an uncomfortable conversation.
Somebody's wandering heart is worth reaching.
Somebody who appears perfectly fine may be quietly losing a war nobody knows they are fighting.
And perhaps today, that somebody is you.
If it is…
hear Paul again.
Not as an angry voice pushing you away.
As an alarm sounding before the house burns down.
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε.
Do not be misled.
Wake up.
Turn around.
Come back to Christ.
The risen Jesus is still greater than the road that led you away.
And remember this when the voices around you become louder than the Voice that called you:
Be careful who gets close enough to rewrite your convictions—because only Jesus deserves to rewrite your life.
